rubrics_metrics.name: Parody / Fair Use defense (copyright/publicity suits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody is protected by the First Amendment and can support a fair use defense in copyright/publicity litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As described in Burnett v. Twentieth Century Fox Film Corporation, the court ruled in favor of the defendant because the bit was a parody, which is protected by the First Amendment, particularly by the Fair Use doctrine. The episode 'put a cartoon version of Carol Burnett/the Charwoman in an awkward, ridiculous, crude, and absurd situation in order to lampoon and parody her as a public figure. Accordingly, the Court finds this factor weighs in favor of fair use.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabloid libel and retraction outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: False tabloid allegations can give rise to libel suits and monetary awards, though awards may be reduced on appeal or settled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The National Enquirer published a false article about Burnett, later retracted it, and Burnett sued for libel. She ultimately won a judgment (initial jury award of $1.6 million reduced to $200,000 after appeals) and a final settlement. The episode is described as a historic victory for libel victims of tabloid journalism.
